text:
ROXANE:
  Not a word! . . .
  (She goes back inside and closes the door again.)

CYRANO (bowing to her, once the door is closed):
  Thank you.
  (The door opens again and Roxane puts her head out.)

ROXANE:
  He might be preparing himself! . . .

CYRANO:
  Good heavens, no! . . .

BOTH (together):
  Hush! . . .
  (The door closes.)

CYRANO (calling):
  Christian!



Scene 3.IV.

Cyrano, Christian.


CYRANO:
  I know everything that is needed. Prepare your memory.
  Here is the opportunity to cover oneself with glory.
  Let us waste no time. Do not look so sullen.
  Quickly, let us go back to your place; I am going to teach you. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  No! I am waiting for Roxane here.

CYRANO:
  What madness
  Has seized you? Come quickly and learn. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  No, I tell you!
  I am tired of borrowing my letters, my speeches,
  And of playing this role, and of always trembling! . . .
  It was fine at first! But I feel that she loves me!
  Thank you. I am no longer afraid. I am going to speak for myself.

CYRANO:
  Oh, really!

CHRISTIAN:
  And who tells you that I would not know how? . . .
  I am not so stupid, after all! You will see!
  But, my dear fellow, your lessons have been useful to me.
  I shall know how to speak on my own! And, by all the devils,
  I shall always know well enough how to take her in my arms! . . .
  (Catching sight of Roxane, who is coming out of Clomire's house):
  —There she is! Cyrano, no, do not leave me!

CYRANO (bowing to him):
  Speak on your own, Monsieur.
  (He disappears behind the garden wall.)



Scene 3.V.

Christian, Roxane, several male and female précieuses, and the duenna,
for a moment.


ROXANE (leaving Clomire's house with a company from whom she takes
  her leave, with curtsies and bows):
  Barthénoïde!—Alcandre!—Grémione! . . .

THE DUENNA (in despair):
  We missed the discourse on Tenderness!
  (She goes into Roxane's house.)

ROXANE (still bidding farewell):
  Urimédonte! . . .Farewell! . . .
  (They all bow to Roxane, bow again to one another, part, and
  go off down different streets. Roxane sees Christian):
  It is you! . . .
  (She goes to him):
  Evening is falling.
  Wait. They are far away. The air is mild. Not a passerby.
  Let us sit down. Speak. I am listening.

CHRISTIAN (sits beside her on the bench. A silence):
  I love you.

ROXANE (closing her eyes):
  Yes, speak to me of love.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love you.

ROXANE:
  That is the theme.
  Embroider, embroider.

CHRISTIAN:
  I love. . .

ROXANE:
  Embroider!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love you so much.

ROXANE:
  No doubt! And then?

CHRISTIAN:
  And then. . .I would be so happy
  If you loved me!—Tell me, Roxane, that you love me!

ROXANE (pouting):
  You offer me gruel when I was hoping for creams!
  Tell me a little how you love me? . . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Why. . .very much.

ROXANE:
  Oh! . . .Unlabyrinth your feelings!

CHRISTIAN (who has moved closer and is devouring the fair nape of her neck with his eyes):
  Your neck!
  I would like to kiss it! . . .

ROXANE:
  Christian!

CHRISTIAN:
  I love you!

ROXANE (trying to rise):
  Again!

CHRISTIAN (quickly, holding her back):
  No! I do not love you!

ROXANE (sitting down again):
  That is fortunate!

CHRISTIAN:
  I adore you!

ROXANE (rising and moving away):
  Oh!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes. . .I am becoming a fool!

ROXANE (dryly):
  And that displeases me!
  As it would displease me if you were to become ugly.

CHRISTIAN:
  But. . .

ROXANE:
  Go and gather up your fugitive eloquence!

CHRISTIAN:
  I. . .

ROXANE:
  You love me, I know. Farewell.
  (She goes toward the house.)

CHRISTIAN:
  Not yet!
  I will tell you. . .

ROXANE (pushing the door open to go inside):
  That you adore me. . .yes, I know.
  No! No! Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  But I. . .
  (She shuts the door in his face.)

CYRANO (who came back in some time ago without being seen):
  It is a success.



Scene 3.VI.

Christian, Cyrano, the pages, for a moment.


CHRISTIAN:
  Help!

CYRANO:
  No, Monsieur.

CHRISTIAN:
  I shall die if I do not regain
  Her favor this very instant. . .

CYRANO:
  And how the devil can I
  Teach you this very instant? . . .

CHRISTIAN (seizing his arm):
  Oh! There, look, see!
  (The balcony window has lit up.)

CYRANO (moved):
  Her window!

CHRISTIAN (shouting):
  I am going to die!

CYRANO:
  Lower your voice!

CHRISTIAN (very softly):
  Die! . . .

CYRANO:
  The night is dark. . .

CHRISTIAN:
  Well?

CYRANO:
  It can be repaired.
  You do not deserve it. . .Stand there, wretch!
  There, in front of the balcony! I shall stand beneath it. . .
  And prompt you with your words.

CHRISTIAN:
  But. . .

CYRANO:
  Be quiet!

THE PAGES (reappearing at the back, to Cyrano):
  Hey!

CYRANO:
  Hush! . . .
  (He motions to them to speak softly.)

FIRST PAGE (in a low voice):
  We have just serenaded
  Montfleury! . . .

CYRANO (softly, quickly):
  Go and lie in ambush,
  One at that street corner, and the other at this one;
  And if some troublesome passerby comes this way,
  Play a tune!

SECOND PAGE:
  What kind of tune, Monsieur Gassendist?

CYRANO:
  A merry one for a woman, and for a man, a sad one!
  (The pages disappear, one at each street corner.—To Christian):
  Call her!

CHRISTIAN:
  Roxane!

CYRANO (picking up pebbles and throwing them at the windowpanes):
  Wait! A few pebbles.



Scene VII.

Roxane, Christian, Cyrano, at first hidden beneath the balcony.


ROXANE (partly opening her window):
  Who is calling me, then?

CHRISTIAN:
  Me.

ROXANE:
  Who is “me”?

CHRISTIAN:
  Christian.

ROXANE (disdainfully):
  It is you?

CHRISTIAN:
  I would like to speak to you.

CYRANO (beneath the balcony, to Christian):
  Good. Good. Almost in a whisper.

ROXANE:
  No! You speak too poorly. Go away!

CHRISTIAN:
  Please! . . .

ROXANE:
  No! You no longer love me!

CHRISTIAN (as Cyrano prompts him with the words):
  To accuse me—just gods!—
  Of loving no more. . .when. . .I love more!

ROXANE (who was about to close her window again, stopping):
  Well! That is better!

CHRISTIAN (the same business):
  Love grows, rocked within my anxious soul. . .
  Which that. . .cruel brat took for. . .a cradle!

ROXANE (coming forward onto the balcony):
  That is better!—But since it is cruel, you were foolish
  Not to smother that love in its cradle!
